beats.intro: Chapter seven, lesson two. Membrane proteins and carbohydrates. [[gate]]Think of a border crossing. A fence runs along the line, but the fence alone does very little. The work is done by the gates, the guard booths, the scanners, and the badges people carry. [[cell]]A cell's border works the same way. [[patch]]Here is the patch of membrane we built in lesson one: a fluid sheet of phospholipids. [[lit]]Now we light up the rest of it. The proteins, and the sugar chains. Proteins determine most of the membrane's specific functions.
beats.tour: Here is figure seven seven, a tour of all the parts. [[sides]]The outer face looks out at the extracellular fluid, with the fibres of the {{ECM|E C M}}, the extracellular matrix. The inner face looks into the cytoplasm, where the microfilaments of the cytoskeleton run. [[lipids]]In between, the bilayer, with cholesterol tucked between the tails, as in lesson one. [[prot]]Embedded in it, like tiles in a mosaic, are the proteins. A membrane is a collage of different proteins in the fluid lipid bilayer. [[integral]]This one reaches into the middle of the bilayer: an integral protein. [[periph]]These are only stuck to the surface, here on the cytoplasmic side: peripheral proteins. [[glyco]]And on the outer face, short chains of sugar. A chain on a protein makes a glycoprotein. A chain on a lipid makes a glycolipid.
beats.kinds: Let's sort the proteins by where they sit. [[periph]]Peripheral proteins are bound to the surface of the membrane. They never enter the core of the bilayer. [[integral]]Integral proteins penetrate the hydrophobic core, the water-avoiding middle where the gold tails are. [[trans]]Many of them go all the way through, from one side to the other. An integral protein that spans the membrane is called a transmembrane protein. [[helix]]Now look at the part inside the core. It is one or more stretches of nonpolar amino acids, often coiled into a spiral called an alpha helix. [[why]]Why nonpolar? Because the core is made of fatty acid tails, which avoid water. Nonpolar amino acids are comfortable there, so the protein stays put in the membrane.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which part is which?
beats.funcs: Membrane proteins do six major jobs. [[list]]Transport. Enzymatic activity. Signal transduction. Cell to cell recognition. Intercellular joining. And attachment to the cytoskeleton and the extracellular matrix. [[a]]First, transport. A passage through the membrane lets a substance cross, and it needs no {{ATP|A T P}}. A different protein uses {{ATP|A T P}} to push a substance across. Lesson five names them. [[b]]Second, enzymatic activity. An enzyme in the membrane speeds up a reaction, right on the membrane surface. [[c]]Third, signal transduction. A signaling molecule, outside the cell, binds to a receptor. The receptor passes the message to the inside, and the cell responds. The signaling molecule itself never has to enter. [[d]]Fourth, cell to cell recognition. A glycoprotein's sugar chain acts like an identity badge, which a neighbouring cell can read. [[e]]Fifth, intercellular joining. Proteins of two neighbouring cells hook together, and hold the cells side by side, like the junctions you saw in chapter six. [[f]]And sixth, attachment. A protein ties the cytoskeleton on the inside to the fibres of the {{ECM|E C M}} on the outside.
beats.q2: Quick check. Match each job to a membrane protein.
beats.carbs: Back to the sugar chains, because they carry the identity badge. [[chains]]Cells recognise each other by binding to molecules on their surface, often carbohydrates. [[bond]]Each chain is covalently bonded to something in the membrane. If it is bonded to a lipid, we call it a glycolipid. If it is bonded to a protein, a glycoprotein, and that is the more common kind. [[face]]They sit only on the external side of the membrane, facing outward, where other cells can touch them. [[vary]]And the chains differ. They vary from species to species, from one individual to another, and even between different types of cells in the same body. [[badge]]That variety is what makes them useful as badges. So cells can tell who is who.
beats.example: Let's put all six jobs on one cell. [[cellrow]]Here is one cell, and its membrane. [[msg]]A signaling molecule arrives and binds the receptor. The message passes inside. That is signal transduction. [[pass]]A passage opens, and a substance crosses with no energy spent. Beside it, a protein spends {{ATP|A T P}}. Transport. [[enz]]An enzyme works on the inner surface. [[neigh]]A neighbouring cell comes close. It reads the sugar chains, and finds they match. Recognition. Then the proteins join the two cells together. [[hold]]Attachment holds the cell in place, to the matrix outside and the filaments inside. [[note]]One membrane, and six jobs, done by proteins.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]A membrane is a collage of proteins in a fluid bilayer, and proteins give it most of its specific functions. [[w2]]Peripheral proteins sit on the surface. Integral proteins penetrate the core, and transmembrane ones span it, with nonpolar helices inside. [[w3]]The six jobs are transport, enzymes, signaling, recognition, joining, and attachment. [[w4]]And sugar chains, on glycoproteins and glycolipids, face outward, and work as identity badges. [[end]]Now try the practice.
